pages.title: Part 1: Volume Terminology, Volume-Load Calculations, and Work Equivalencies
pages.readingHtml:
Volume Terminology and Volume-Load Calculations

In resistance program design, volume relates to the total amount of weight lifted in a training session, serving as a primary determinant of metabolic expenditure and neuromuscular stress. A set is defined as a group of repetitions sequentially performed before the athlete stops to rest. Understanding and accurately quantifying training volume requires distinguishing between two distinct metrics:

  • Repetition-Volume: The total number of repetitions performed during a single workout session across all exercises.
  • Volume-Load: The total number of sets multiplied by the number of repetitions per set, then multiplied by the weight lifted per repetition ($ ext{Volume-Load} = ext{Sets} imes ext{Repetitions} imes ext{Weight}$).

For example, if an athlete performs 2 sets of 10 repetitions with 50 pounds ($23 ext{ kg}$), the volume-load is calculated as $2 imes 10 imes 50 ext{ lb} = 1,000 ext{ pounds}$ ($454 ext{ kg}$). If different sets within an exercise or session are performed with varying weights, the volume-loads per individual set are calculated separately and then summed to determine the total session volume-load.

Concentric Work and Average Load per Repetition

Multiplying volume-load by the vertical displacement factor of the weight during each repetition yields the total concentric mechanical work performed. Because vertical displacement is relatively constant for a given athlete across standard exercises, it is omitted in daily calculations; however, volume-load remains directly proportional to total mechanical work.

Dividing total volume-load by repetition-volume yields the average weight lifted per repetition ($ ext{Average Weight} = rac{ ext{Volume-Load}}{ ext{Repetition-Volume}}$). This calculated average provides a valuable proxy for training intensity and the overall quality of work executed during the session.

Cross-Disciplinary Mechanical Work Equivalencies

The concept of volume-load in resistance training shares direct physiological equivalencies with volume measures across other athletic disciplines:

  • Running & Aerobic Training: Repetition-volume is quantified by distance. When combined with an intensity metric (such as running pace or $\%V\dot{O}_2 ext{max}$), total metabolic energy cost (proportional to mechanical work) can be derived, serving as the direct equivalent of volume-load.
  • Plyometric Training: Volume is quantified by the total number of foot contacts (for lower body drills) or hand contacts (for upper body drills).
  • Swimming & Rowing: Volume is quantified by the total number of stroke cycles or total distance covered.
  • Sport-Specific Skill Practice: Volume is measured by the total number of throws, jumps, or skill attempts performed per session.
Coaching / Sport Application

Strength and conditioning professionals must track volume-load rather than simple set or repetition counts to monitor overall mechanical work and fatigue. Dividing total volume-load by repetition-volume allows coaches to calculate the average load per repetition, ensuring that training intensity matches the intended microcycle goal.

Volume-Load $ ext{Sets} imes ext{Reps} imes ext{Weight}$ Proportional to concentric work and metabolic cost Total energy expenditure ($ ext{Pace} imes ext{Distance}$)

pages.title: Part 2: Single vs. Multiple Sets and Athlete Training Status
pages.readingHtml:
Single vs. Multiple Set Resistance Training Debates

A longstanding debate in exercise prescription centers on whether performing single sets or multiple sets per exercise is optimal for strength and hypertrophy. Some researchers have advocated that performing one set of 8 to 12 repetitions to volitional muscular failure (after warm-up) is sufficient to maximize gains in muscular strength and hypertrophy. Research demonstrates that untrained individuals can indeed achieve significant strength increases using single-set routines during the initial several months of training.

However, overwhelming evidence indicates that higher training volumes are necessary to promote continued adaptation, particularly in intermediate and advanced resistance-trained athletes. Over time, the musculoskeletal system adapts to the stimulus of a single set to failure, requiring the progressive addition of multiple sets to drive further strength gains.

Physiological Comparison of Set Volume and Fatigue

Comparative training studies reveal important physiological distinctions between single-set and multiple-set protocols:

  • Submaximal Multiple Sets vs. Single Sets to Failure: Research demonstrates that performing 3 sets of 10 repetitions without going to failure produces significantly greater strength gains than performing 1 set of 8 to 12 repetitions to failure. The higher total training volume provided by 3 sets is the primary contributing factor to superior strength adaptation.
  • Accelerated Adaptation: Athletes who perform multiple sets from the initiation of their resistance training program increase muscular strength at a significantly faster rate than those utilizing single-set protocols.
  • Accumulative Fatigue Kinetics: Strength coaches cannot expect athletes to maintain full RM loads across fixed repetition schemes for every set in a session. Accumulative fatigue impairs motor unit firing rates and metabolic recovery, reducing the maximum repetitions achievable in later sets unless load is adjusted or rest intervals are extended.

Influence of Training Status on Volume Tolerance

An athlete's training status directly dictates the volume of work they can safely tolerate and adapt to without experiencing overtraining:

  1. Untrained / Beginner Athletes: Should initiate training with 1 or 2 sets per exercise. This conservative volume minimizes delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS) and allows structural connective tissue adaptation.
  2. Intermediate / Advanced Athletes: Require a gradual progression to 3–6 sets per exercise to match the specific guidelines associated with their primary training goal.
Coaching / Sport Application

While single-set training may produce initial strength gains in beginners, strength professionals must transition athletes to multiple-set programs (3 to 6 sets per exercise) for long-term adaptation. Furthermore, coaches must account for accumulative set fatigue by anticipating load reductions or managing rest intervals across consecutive sets.

Training Volume ProtocolTarget PopulationPrimary Adaptation RateKey Physiological Rationale
Single-Set (1 set to failure) Untrained beginners (first 1–3 months)Moderate initial strength gainsMinimal volume sufficient for unadapted neuromuscular system
Multiple Submaximal Sets (3 sets of 10) Intermediate to advanced athletesAccelerated, superior strength gainsHigher total volume-load drives greater motor unit recruitment
Multiple Max-RM Sets Trained athletes (power/strength focus)Maximal strength supercompensationHigh volume-load at high intensity; requires fatigue management

pages.title: Part 3: Assigning Volume by Primary Training Goal
pages.readingHtml:
Assigning Volume Based on Primary Training Goals

Training volume is directly dictated by the athlete's primary resistance training goal. According to Table 17.11 in the NSCA guidelines, specific repetition and set ranges are assigned to optimize adaptations for strength, power, hypertrophy, and muscular endurance.

1. Strength Training Volume Guidelines

Historical research by DeLorme and Watkins originally recommended sets of 10 repetitions for strength, though this was developed for injury rehabilitation. Subsequent research by Berger suggested 3 sets of 6 repetitions produced maximal strength gains. Further studies found similar strength increases across 6 sets of 2RM, 3 sets of 6RM, and 3 sets of 10RM in untrained subjects. However, for trained athletes, maximal strength gains require:

  • Repetition Range: 6 or fewer repetitions per set.
  • Set Volume for Core Exercises: 2 to 5 sets or 3 to 6 sets per core exercise.
  • Set Volume for Assistance Exercises: 1 to 3 sets per assistance exercise are generally sufficient.

2. Power Training Volume Guidelines

Volume assignments for power training are typically lower than those for maximal strength training to maintain maximal movement velocity and explosive exercise quality:

  • Repetition Range: 1 to 2 repetitions for single-effort power events (e.g., shot put, high jump); 3 to 5 repetitions for multiple-effort power sports (e.g., basketball, volleyball).
  • Set Volume: 3 to 5 sets per power exercise (after warm-up).
  • Velocity Rationale: Lower repetition counts prevent fatigue-induced reductions in movement speed and rate of force development ($ ext{RFD}$).

3. Hypertrophy Training Volume Guidelines

Higher total training volumes are mandatory to drive myofibrillar protein synthesis and muscle cell enlargement:

  • Repetition Range: 6 to 12 repetitions per set.
  • Set Volume per Exercise: 3 to 6 sets per exercise.
  • Number of Exercises: Performing 3 or more exercises per targeted muscle group is the most effective strategy to maximize muscle size, creating a substantial cumulative volume-load.

4. Muscular Endurance Training Volume Guidelines

Muscular endurance programs emphasize high-repetition work to enhance local metabolic capacity and fatigue resistance:

  • Repetition Range: 12 or more repetitions per set.
  • Set Volume: 2 to 3 sets per exercise.
  • Volume-Load Balance: Although repetition volume is high ($\ge 12$ reps), overall volume-load remains moderate because lighter loads ($\le 67\% ext{ 1RM}$) and fewer sets are performed.
Coaching / Sport Application

Strength coaches must strictly align volume prescription with the targeted adaptive goal: assign $\le 6$ reps and 2–6 sets for strength, 1–5 reps and 3–5 sets for power, 6–12 reps and 3–6 sets (with $\ge 3$ exercises per muscle group) for hypertrophy, and $\ge 12$ reps and 2–3 sets for muscular endurance.

glossary.def: The total amount of weight lifted or total mechanical work performed during a resistance training session.
A group of repetitions sequentially performed before an athlete stops to rest.
The total number of repetitions performed during a workout session across all exercises.
The total mathematical product of sets, repetitions per set, and weight lifted per repetition (Sets x Repetitions x Weight).
The mechanical work performed during muscle shortening, calculated as volume-load multiplied by vertical displacement distance.
Total volume-load divided by repetition-volume, serving as a quantitative proxy for session intensity and work quality.
Performing one set of an exercise to volitional failure; effective for beginners but insufficient for long-term trained athlete adaptation.
Performing two or more sets per exercise; essential for intermediate and advanced athletes to drive continued strength and hypertrophy.
A high-volume protocol prescribing 6 to 12 repetitions for 3 to 6 sets across 3 or more exercises per targeted muscle group.
A high-repetition protocol prescribing 12 or more repetitions for 2 to 3 sets with submaximal loads (<= 67% 1RM).
